text:
Moth and Gravel Field Note 3. A
metaphor has to earn its place.

An AI narrated edition of the
published note.

A river is an interesting way to
show a week. You come back to a

project after a day away. Some
work has landed. A decision has

changed. Someone needs an
answer. Before doing anything

else, you need to recover the
shape of what happened. Decision

Docket is our own tool in
production for our own work. It

is concerned with that return,
finding the reason behind a

decision and continuing with the
relevant context. This note

follows one part of its design
work. The attempt to give that

experience a distinctive form on
Android. A river offers a useful

starting point. Time gives it
direction. Changes give each

stretch something to inspect.
Decisions and handoffs can

become recognizable marks. Touch
a day and the corresponding work

comes into view. The attraction
is easy to understand. The

responsibility takes longer. O1
River A period to inspect. Find

a stretch of time. Read the work
that belongs to it. O2 Circle A

perspective to choose. Bring one
view forward. Keep its context

close. O3 Focus One thing to
read. Stay with a change. Leave

a place to continue. Reading
models, conceptual diagrams, not

application screenshots. The
picture has to explain

something. In Docket's web
recap, the river is wider where

more work landed or changed.
That is a way of showing

observed activity. The reader
still needs titles, dates, and

source context to understand
what it means. One distinction

matters especially. The past and
the present need different

places. Selecting Friday's
history should never make

today's unanswered question
disappear. A beautiful filter

would be a poor one if it taught
a person that the work no longer

needed them. This is where a
visual metaphor earns its place.

It helps someone orient
themselves, then makes the

relevant detail easier to reach.
Shape carries meaning. Words

keep that meaning accountable. A
circle gives a perspective a

place. Circle approaches the
same material from another

direction. Six familiar roles
sit around a table. Choose a

perspective and bring it
forward, then read the work

associated with it. The web
recap uses those roles to

present existing categories of
work. Their character should

never suggest a conversation
authorship or live presence that

the underlying information does
not establish. For the Android

experiment, the selected
question appears beneath the

scene in a speech bubble
connected to the front seat. The

question should be close enough
to act on without covering

another perspective or turning
the page into a diagram that

must be decoded. The turn can
help connect a choice to its

result. The ordinary list has to
carry the same work. Both belong

to the design. More realism did
not settle the problem. An early

revision pursued depth through
photographic material. A more

literal table for circle and a
pebble riverbed for river. That

artwork was rejected. The
literal furniture and river

scenery pulled away from the
product's a established persona

illustrations. Adding material
detail had not made the

interface more coherent. The
following study removed those

photographs and tried a shared
vocabulary of thin ceramic

surfaces, soft water, restrained
edges, and contact shadows. The

personas and the questions
remained. The execution changed.

That is an iteration, not a
verdict. A new drawing can

resolve a visible mismatch while
leaving the more important

question open. Does a person
find the right context and

understand what to do next?
River slash the period in view.

Actual Android emulator capture,
Docket light. Synthetic demo

work, revision 86B6A90A. Circle
slash a question close at hand.

Actual Android emulator capture,
Docket light. Synthetic demo

work, revision A505C66F.
Captured on the 12th of October

2026 in incomplete validation
runs. These images show the

native rendering. The
interaction and physical device

checks remain open. Open either
image to inspect the full

capture. A phone changes the
contract. The native experiment

compares river, circle, and
focus using the same synthetic

changes and questions. Focus
offers one change at a time with

explicit previous and next
controls alongside its pager.

Giving each direction the same
work makes the comparison more

useful. On a phone, a gesture
has neighbors. A drag through

the river lives beside vertical
scrolling and the system's back

gesture. A question sheet lives
beside the keyboard, rotation,

and the possibility that the app
goes into the background. Those

are design materials too. The
prototype therefore separates

looking, choosing, and
committing. Swiping changes the

visible item. Selecting an
answer prepares a choice. An

explicit action commits it.
Pending, unknown, and recorded

results have distinct
presentations because they

describe different things the
person needs to understand. This

is a native experiment, not a
silent replacement of the web

reply behavior. The phone needs
its own account of interruption

and return. The useful part has
to survive the spectacle.

A reduced motion setting should
keep every selection and every

question. Large text should have
room to breathe. A list or a

labeled day control should let
someone complete the same task

without learning the drawing's
gestures. There is still work to

do. The Android build and lint
checks have passed, but the full

native interaction and physical
phone accessibility walk are

incomplete. Emulator failures
have interrupted capture. The

newer forms have not earned a
claim of measured phone

performance or final usability.
The next meaningful comparison

is concrete. Find why a decision
was made, inspect a change,

prepare an answer, and back
away. Return to finish, then

save a place and reopen it.
Watch the wrong turns. Ask what

the person believes happened
when an outcome is uncertain. A

memorable river or circle might
make the work feel more

approachable. It earns its place
when someone comes back, finds

their footing, and continues.
You have been listening to Moth

and Gravel Field Notes. The
written edition is at
mothandgravel.com.
